20087-the-pony-rider-boys-in-texas-or-th:
Frank Gee Patchin published The Pony Rider Boys in Texas in 1910. Its subtitle is The Veiled Riddle of the Plains. A freckle-faced boy sits his pony with easy skill in San Diego, Texas. Crowds surge and shout along the main street around him.

The Pony Rider Boys roam the West in a long, loved boys' series. Each book drops them into a new state, ranch, or wild scrape. Texas gives them heat, cattle country, and a riddle to solve. Readers get fast action, camp craft, and friendship tested on the plains.
20299-unwritten-literature-of-hawaii-the:
Unwritten Literature of Hawaii gathers the sacred songs of the hula. Most of the book holds Hawaiian songs used in the hula for ages. Those songs formed the stock supply of dancers and chanters. Descriptive parts were added to give the songs their proper setting.

Such notes answer the questions of readers new to Hawaiian custom. The songs praise gods, chiefs, places, and the forces of nature. Printing them saved oral art that lived only in trained memory. Readers get a key record of Hawaiian poetry and sacred dance. Chanters trained for years to hold these long songs exactly in memory.
20535-the-merry-thought-or-the-glass-win:
The Merry Thought, or the Glass Window and Bog-House Miscellany, has been called the strangest anthology of the eighteenth century. It collects verses that wits scratched on window glass and worse places. A modern study introduces the pieces and their odd literary worth.

The study gives Samuel Johnson's mad play Hurlothrumbo as a kindred case. It may be mostly nonsense, the writer grants, but as literary history it is highly significant nonsense. The play revolted against all stage rules and shared many qualities with graffiti. The miscellany itself shows the same spirit at work.
20558-the-merry-thought-or-the-glass-win:
The Merry Thought, or the Glass Window and Bog-House Miscellany, is a 1730s collection of verses scratched by wits on window panes and privy walls. A modern editor studies the collection and its strange company. Great names appear beside the rudest rhymes.

John Donne's poem A Valediction: of My Name in the Window gives the editor a starting point. In it, two lovers face a parting like a scene the editor quotes from Moll Flanders. Using a diamond, the poet writes his name in the glass before a long journey. The study follows that art of window writing through the miscellany's pages.
20723-little-cinderella:
Cinderella sits in the chimney corner among the cinders, and that low place gives her the name her sisters use. Even in shabby clothes, the old tale says, she looks ten times fairer than her sisters in their fine dress. Few fairy tales are as widely known as this one.

In this short telling, a kind and patient girl is kept down by her own household, yet her worth still shows. The contrast between rags and real worth drives the whole story. Young readers get the classic plot in brief, clear form, with its old lesson that good nature can outshine fine clothes.
21506-the-young-llanero-a-story-of-war-a:
Snow peaks of the Andes rise over Venezuela in W. H. G. Kingston's The Young Llanero. A llanero is a horseman of the great plains, and war sweeps those plains in the tale. Kingston returns to South America, a ground he handled well.

Spanish troops, Indigenous peoples, and huge snakes share the action with a kind priest and a doctor. The Orinoco, the land's great river, shapes the travel and the fights. Forty-four engravings graced the printed book, many of high quality. Readers get wild life and war together, in Kingston's brisk and knowing manner.
22515-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
The Modern Scottish Minstrel collects the songs of Scotland across six volumes. Its plan differs from every previous collection of Scottish song. Esteemed lyrics are printed along with memoirs of their authors.

The poets' names stand arranged in chronological order throughout. Those counted modern lived into the past half-century before publication. All such poets are included in the work's wide sweep. Song and life thus explain each other on the page. Readers can trace Scottish song through its makers' own stories. The set preserves hundreds of lyrics that might else have scattered. It remains a treasury for singers, scholars, and Scots abroad.
23299-stradella:
Stradella is a historical tale of music and courts in old Italy. One figure in it is a man of culture and refined tastes, fond of music above much else. He writes sonnets, reads the elegant Politian, and composes sentimental airs for voice and lute in his spare hours.

He won vast credit as a patron of arts and letters, at very secret small cost. Poets, musicians, and artists who paid court to him, and dedicated their choicest works to him, got nothing more than a supper and a recommendation. Readers get a story of the singer Stradella's world: brilliance, flattery, and patrons who praise freely and pay carefully.
682-catalan-s-constant-ramanujan-s-formu:
This volume prints Catalan's constant to three hundred thousand digits, computed in 1996 by Thomas Papanikolaou on a Sun Ultra-Sparc in about a day and eight hours. A short program fronts the digits, using a standard series sped by an Euler transform and the LiDIA library. Notes recall earlier records of two hundred thousand and one hundred thousand digits. The constant itself is given as a sum over odd squares.

The book serves less as reading than as a reference store for mathematicians and coders, who can test software against its long, checked digits. Its record-setting run marks a moment in computing history. For most readers it stands as a monument to precision, where a single strange number fills pages.
728-emile-zola:
William Dean Howells wrote this tribute weeks after the death of Emile Zola, the French novelist of great moral force. He argues that history now forms its view fast, and that Zola can already be judged as fairly as past heroes. Howells praises Zola's epic imagination and his ethical drive, the same powers that made his novels both art and protest.

The essay is short, warm, and clear, written by an American peer who admired French realism without copying it. It sets Zola's life and work in the public events of his day, above all the Dreyfus affair that made him a public conscience. For new readers, it is a fine first guide to why Zola mattered beyond France.
a-woman-s-life-work-labors-and-experienc:
Laura S. Haviland wrote her memoir at seventy-three and dated the preface October 1881, apologizing for plain, unvarnished facts in place of eloquence. A Woman's Life-Work tells how a Quaker farm wife in Michigan became a tireless worker for the enslaved, the poor, and the prisoner, driven by sympathies she says she could not refuse.

Early chapters cover childhood, marriage, removal to Michigan, bereavement, and early widowhood. She goes on to describe founding the Raisin Institute, aiding fugitives, and decades of visiting, teaching, and relief work. The tone is devout and practical at once: every chapter measures faith by labor done for people in trouble, which is the record she wanted left behind.
ballades-rhymes-from-ballades-in-blue-ch:
Andrew Lang published his Ballades in Blue China in 1880 and Rhymes a la Mode five years later; this Longmans volume of 1911 draws its contents from both. The title page signs him simply A. Lang. The contents are a roll of ballades on his ruling pleasures: Theocritus, Cleopatra's Needle, roulette, sleep, the Tweed, and the book-hunter.

Lang helped revive the old French fixed forms in English, and the ballade's refrain and envoi are his playground here. There is a ballade of the royal game of golf, a double ballade of primitive man, and a version of Villon's Ballade of Good Counsel. The Blue China ballade itself celebrates the willow-pattern plate. Rhymes a la Mode adds slighter society verse. The whole is light verse of high finish, written to look easy.
camilla: Camilla, Fanny Burney's novel. Another edition. This book preserves that classic. It waits for future eyes. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
carmilla:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu, an Irish master of the ghost tale, wrote this vampire tale in 1872. It came out a full twenty six years before Stoker's Dracula. Le Fanu set his tale in Styria, a lone land of woods and ruined keeps in Austria.

A young girl, Laura, tells how the fair Carmilla came to stay in her home. By slow steps the guest is shown to be a vampire who feeds on her hosts in the night. The tale made the female vampire a set form in books, and its dread is all the more strong for its calm.
catalan-s-constant-ramanujan-s-formula:
Greg Fee computed Catalan's constant to 300,000 digits on September 29, 1996, using a Sun Ultra-Sparc workstation, and this file prints the result. The headnote says the run took one day, eight hours, and a quarter hour more. Catalan's constant appears in series in mathematics and has no known simple closed form.

Fee used the standard series for the constant, sped up with an Euler transform, a method that makes a slow series converge faster. The program drew on LiDIA, a software library for computational number theory, using its multi-precision arithmetic. The body of the file is the digits themselves, block after block, offered as a reference value for mathematicians checking their own computations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abila: Abila, a Phoenician titular see in the Mount Lebanon region, is today Suk Wady Barada, near Damascus, once Abilina's capital and stronghold, named in Luke 3:1. The notice ties the ancient bishopric to the district of Abilina around it and places the old see in its modern setting. It gives a location and a scriptural anchor, and nothing more, for readers tracing the ancient sees of the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelia-flaccil:
Aelia Flaccilla was empress and wife of Theodosius the Great, who died about 385 or 386. Like Theodosius, she was of Spanish descent, and may have been daughter of Claudius Antonius, Prefect of Gaul and consul in 382. Her marriage to Theodosius probably took place in 376. That year his father fell into disfavour and he withdrew to Cauca in Gallaecia. Her eldest son, later Emperor Arcadius, was born late the next year.

She bore two more children: Honorius in 384, and Pulcheria, dead young, shortly before her mother. Three children is Gregory of Nyssa's count, so the Gratian named by St. Ambrose, with Pulcheria, was probably not her son. Like her husband, Flaccilla zealously supported the Nicene Creed and blocked a conference between emperor and the Arian Eunomius. On the throne she shone as a model of Christian virtue and ardent charity. Ambrose and Gregory praised her alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-agr:
Alexander Agricola was a celebrated composer of the fifteenth century and a pupil of Okeghem, of Belgian or, by other accounts, German origin. Born about 1446 and educated in the Netherlands, he was a fine singer and performer even in youth. Until 1474 he sang in the ducal chapel at Milan. He then served the Duke of Mantua and Philip, Duke of Austria and King of the Netherlands, following Philip to Castile in 1505.

Agricola died at Valladolid in 1506, aged sixty, and stood in high esteem as a composer. Many of his works are believed still to lie unpublished in Spanish libraries. Of those published, Petrucci printed thirty-one songs and motets in 1502 to 1503, along with a volume of five masses, including Le Serviteur, Je ne demande, and Malheur me bat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquila:
Aquila is an Italian archdiocese in the Abruzzi, directly subject to the Holy See. The see of Forconium came first, in 680, and the diocese of Aquila was founded by Alexander IV on 20 February 1257. Pius VII joined the suppressed see of Cittàducale to it in 1818, and Pius IX made it an archdiocese on 23 January 1876. Its figures run to 107,800 Catholics, 135 parishes, and 217 secular priests, twenty-nine regulars, 130 seminarians, and 264 churches or chapels.

The town stands high in the mountains, with broad straight streets and fine churches, its cathedral dedicated to Saints Maximus and George. The body of Bernardine of Siena, who died at Aquila, is kept in a church built in his honour. Celestine V was buried there in 1296 at Collemaggio, where he was made pope. Three earthquakes struck the town, and in the 2 February 1703 quake over two thousand died, eight hundred of them in St. Dominic's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquila-and-pr:
Aquila and Priscilla, or Prisca, were Jewish tentmakers who left Rome, Aquila, a Pontus native, in the Jewish persecution under Claudius in 49 or 50. They settled at Corinth, where they hosted Paul, a fellow tentmaker, on his first visit. When they converted is not known. They travelled with Paul to Ephesus, instructed the Alexandrian Apollos, hosted Paul at Ephesus for three years on his third missionary journey, and kept a Christian church in their house.

They left Ephesus for Rome, likely after the riot stirred by the silversmith Demetrius. They kept a house church at Rome too, then left again, probably under Nero's persecution, and settled once more at Ephesus. The Roman Martyrology, the calendar of saints, commemorates them on 8 July. Scripture several times names Priscilla before Aquila, for reasons the article rehearses, and modern difficulties raised by their frequent moves are addressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arindela: Arindela was a titular see in Palestine, a former bishop's seat now given as a title. Its bishops' list from 431 to 536 is given in Gams, on page 454 of his work. The entry is a single gazetteer line, recording the see's place in Palestine and the years covered by its known bishops, with no further history attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascoli-satria:
Ascoli Satriano and Cirignola form an Italian diocese, suffragan to Beneventum's archdiocese, covering six towns and two villages in Foggia province. In 969 Ausculum Appulum emerges as an episcopal city among Beneventum's suffragans, but the first bishop known to us is Maurus, present at the consecration of St. Angelo's church at Volturno in 1059. Cirignola, by its relative importance, must once have been a diocese, but history is silent on it.

When Pius VII reorganized the Neapolitan kingdom's provinces under the Concordat of 16 February 1818 with Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, their king, he restored Cirignola to ancient episcopal dignity. He united it equally with Ascoli. At the end of 1905 the diocese held eleven parishes, sixty-two churches, chapels, and oratories, ninety-eight secular priests, and sixty seminarians. It also held eight regular clergy, four lay brothers, forty-six women religious, and eighteen confraternities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ave-maris-ste:
Ave Maris Stella, meaning Hail, Star of Ocean, is the first verse of an unrhymed, accentual hymn. The hymn holds seven strophes of four lines each. The Roman Breviary assigns it to Vespers in the Common office, the Saturday office, and the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin, as well as to her feasts. It has often been ascribed to St Bernard, but wrongly, since it predates him.

A St Gall manuscript of the ninth century already holds it, and an ascription to Venantius Fortunatus, who died in 609, lacks sufficient authority. Its constant place in the Divine Office made it hugely popular in the Middle Ages. Many later hymns drew on it, borrowing its star-of-the-sea image for Mary. The entry is short, fixing the hymn's form, use, and true age against two false attributions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avila:
Avila, ancient Abula, is a diocese suffragan to Valladolid in Spain, whose bishops run at least from the fourth century, with a claim to apostolic origin. Suppressed during the ninth century, it was restored early in the twelfth after the Moors were expelled, answering to Merida until 1120 and then to Compostella until 1857. It counts 189,926 Catholics, with 360 priests, 339 parishes, and about five hundred churches and chapels.

Avila ranks among the most important cities in Spain's medieval and modern history. In the fourth century the arch-heretic Priscillian held its bishopric, and later saints made it home, among them St Teresa and John of Avila, the Apostle of Andalusia. Once one of Spain's most flourishing cities, its population has shrunk to seven thousand. Its Moorish castle and ancient eleventh-century cathedral stand as monumental relics of the past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-co:
Bernard of Compostella, called Antiquus to set him apart from a namesake, was an early thirteenth-century canonist, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. A native of Compostella in Spain, he became professor of canon law at Bologna. His work gathered the decrees of Innocent III from the first ten years of that pope's reign, 1198 to 1208.

Bologna scholars called it the Roman Compilation, since its documents came from the Roman archives. An official collection reaching to 1210 soon made it superfluous in practice, and only parts survive. The entry is a short note on a scholar's labour overtaken by an official book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biella:
Biella, a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covers an industrial city of Piedmont and its diocese of about 200,000 people. Anciently Bugelia, in the province of Novara, it stands as suffragan to the Archdiocese of Vercelli. Until 1772 it had no bishop of its own, living under Vercelli's rule.

In that year Clement XI, at King Charles Emmanuel III's wish, raised Biella to a diocese by the bull Praecipua, with Giulio Cesare Viancino as first bishop. Napoleon suppressed it in 1803, and it later revived. The entry lists bishops, parishes, and the woollen industry that made the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-of-av:
Blessed John of Avila, apostolic preacher of Andalusia, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Almodóvar del Campo in 1500, he died at Montilla in 1569. Sent to Salamanca at fourteen to study law, he left after a year in distaste for jurisprudence and spent three years in austere piety at home.

A passing Franciscan sent him to Alcalá for philosophy and theology under the Dominican Soto. Ordained, he preached across Andalusia, formed priests, and wrote spiritual works, including Audi, filia, a guide for the devout. The entry presents a preacher whose sermons reformed a region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cagli-e-pergo:
Cagli e Pergola is a diocese in Umbria, under Urbino, whose chief city Cagli was the old Roman colony of Callium. Its first known bishop, Gratianus, attended the Council of Rimini in 359, and later bishops appear at Rome in 500 and 751. Saint Ranieri governed Cagli from 1156 to 1175 before moving to Spalato, where Slavs killed him in 1180 for claiming church lands.

Civil strife between Ghibellines and Guelphs left the see vacant for years after 1276. After a massacre its own citizens burned Cagli and rebuilt it on the plain of Saint Angelo. The cathedral's first stone was laid in 1297 and the building finished in 1398. In 1817 Pergola joined Cagli as an episcopal city, and the diocese now counts 30,000 Catholics in 51 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camillo-mazze:
Camillo Mazzella, theologian and cardinal, was born at Vitulano on 10 February 1833 and died at Rome on 26 March 1900. He entered the Benevento seminary about age eleven, was ordained in September 1855 with a dispensation for youth, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1857. Driven from Italy with the Jesuits in 1860, he taught at Fourvières. He then came to America in 1867, teaching at Georgetown and serving as prefect of studies at Woodstock College.

At Woodstock he published four volumes on religion and the Church, God the Creator, the grace of Christ, and the infused virtues, which ran through several editions. Called to Rome by Leo XIII in 1878 to teach at the Gregorian University, he became a cardinal deacon in 1886. Ten years later he became a cardinal priest, and in 1897 cardinal bishop of Palestrina, the first Jesuit raised to that rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caracalla:
Caracalla, born Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus in 188, ruled Rome as emperor after murdering his brother and co-ruler Geta in 212. He died in 217 near Carrhae in Mesopotamia. Cruel, greedy, and treacherous, he was still a brave soldier and able administrator who campaigned against Germans in the west and enemies in the east to restore the empire's security.

His most notable act extended Roman citizenship to all inhabitants of the empire through the Constitutio Antoniana of 212. The effect on Christians is hard to judge: martyrs could now die as Romans, yet appeal to Caesar ended and heavier taxes followed. Caracalla changed no laws on Christians and kept his father's harsh policy, under which many were put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-castabala:
Castabala was a titular see of Asia Minor whose Latin title was suppressed in 1894. It stood somewhere on the Pyramos River, now the Djihan, in Cilicia, also known as Hieropolis. Perhaps it lay near Osmanie in the Adana province at Kestel or Kastal, five or six miles south of Anazarbus. Other placings, at Karanlik or Kara Kaya, are erroneous. Hierocles and the episcopal lists place it under Anazarbus, the metropolis of Cilicia Secunda.

Around the tenth century it seems to have merged with or been confused with Mamista, or Mopsuestus. Lequien names seven bishops. The first, Maris, is mentioned in an apocryphal letter of Ignatius. Moyses attended Nicaea in 325, Theophilus, a semi-Arian friend of Basil, went on embassy to Rome, and Theodorus attended the Trullan Council in 692.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cella:
A cella was one name for the small memorial chapels sometimes built in early Christian burial grounds, also called memoriae martyrum or confessiones. An inscription from Caesarea in Mauretania records a worshiper of the Word who gave a cemetery ground and built a chapel at his own expense. Archaeologists generally hold that the buildings Pope Fabian ordered in the Roman cemeteries between 236 and 250 were such memorial chapels.

They served chiefly for funeral agapae and anniversaries, when friends of the dead gathered for a Mass for the departed. Two such chapels, dedicated to Sts. Sixtus and Cecilia and to St. Soter, still stand in St. Callistus's cemetery. Many took the form of cellae trichorae: a rectangular nave ending in three semicircular apses, whose chords form three sides of a square.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-r:
An entry on Christopher Royas de Spinola, Bishop of Wiener-Neustadt, born near Roermond in 1626 of a noble Spanish family. Schooled at Cologne, he joined the Franciscans there and taught philosophy and theology. In Spain he became provincial of his order, and in 1661 he escorted Margaret Theresa, first wife of Emperor Leopold the First, to Vienna, where he grew into an influential imperial diplomat.

Spinola became titular Bishop of Knin in 1668 and Bishop of Wiener-Neustadt in January 1686. Backed by Leopold and encouraged by Innocent the Eleventh, he sought reunion with Protestants, treating with Molanus, Calixtus, Leibniz, and the courts of Hanover and Brandenburg. A conference of 1683 seemed to approve his plan, but French influence and his liberal concessions stalled Rome. In 1691 he became commissary-general of reunion in Austria-Hungary, but Rome rejected his extreme terms, including married priests and Mass in German.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compostela:
Fidel Fita y Colomé's entry covers Compostela, a famed city of Spain on a height between the Sar and Sarela rivers. A Celtic castle called Liberum Donum once crowned the hill, and two Roman roads pass below. The see has ranked archiepiscopal since 1120, succeeding ancient Iria, whose bishops run from the fourth century, perhaps the first. Its name appears only from the tenth century, in a document of 912 naming Saint Martin's monastery near the cathedral.

History splits at the 1120 elevation to metropolitan rank. The Sar, swollen by the Sarela, runs some fifteen miles to the Ulla and the sea at Padron. Latin verses quoted here praise Saint James, whose body rests at Compostela, and tell how he first preached to Spanish peoples. The entry closes with Leo XIII's bull of 1 November 1884, confirming Cardinal Payá's declaration on the relics of James, Athanasius, and Theodorus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cupola:
An architectural entry defines the cupola as a rounded ceiling, like a bowl turned upside down, crowning a round, square, or many-sided building. Strictly the term means the underside of a dome, often on a different plane from the dome outside. It is also, without authority, applied to the dome itself and to the small lantern room atop it.

A cupola needs no dome, and domes often crown flat surfaces. Its meaning lies in form, not material or method. San Vitale at Ravenna, made entirely from hollow clay pots set in spiral courses of cement, became the model for centuries in Europe. The Pantheon, Florence Cathedral, St. Peter's, and Hagia Sophia show solid construction on pendentives or drums, while St. Paul's in London pairs masonry with a wooden outer shell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-davila-padill:
A biographical entry presents Agustin Davila Padilla, a Mexican Dominican born in Mexico City in 1562 and dead in 1604. Graduating master of arts at sixteen, he joined the Dominicans. He held philosophy and theology chairs at Puebla and in Mexico. He served as definitor and procurator of his province, and represented it at Rome and Madrid.

Made Bishop of Santo Domingo in 1601, he died there three years later. Though not a prolific writer, he left one very important, if rare, work. It was his History of the Foundation and Discourse of the Province of Santiago de Mexico, published at Madrid in 1596 and Brussels in 1625. Despite mistakes, it remains the leading chronicle of the Dominican Order and its American missions to the end of the sixteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-camp:
Domenico Campagnola was a painter of the Venetian school, born at Padua in 1482, his death date unknown. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry calls him one of the cleverest pupils of Titian's school, so skilled that he is said to have stirred his master's jealousy. He also engraved with mastery in etching and woodcut, and his frescoes may be seen in Padua's Scuola del Santo and in Venice.

His color is fresh and animated, his feeling poetic, his touch easy and brilliant. He is said to have outdone even Titian in daring with the nude figure. A fine panel of Adam and Eve hangs in the Pitti Palace at Florence, and his landscapes so resemble Titian's that they are often given to the master.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-drusilla:
Drusilla was the daughter of Herod Agrippa the First, six years old when her father died at Caesarea in the year 44. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how she was first betrothed to Epiphanes, son of the king of Commagene, on condition that he embrace Judaism. The prince refused his promise, and her brother Agrippa the Second married her to Azizus, king of Emesa, who agreed to circumcision to win her hand.

Not long after, the beautiful young queen met Felix, Rome's procurator of Judea, likely at her brother's court. The entry, drawing on Josephus, notes the jealousy of her elder sister Berenice as a thread in the tale. Of Drusilla's later life after the scene in Acts, nothing is known for sure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavia-domiti:
Flavia Domitilla was a Christian matron of the imperial family near the first century's close. She was the third of three women of that name: grandmother, mother, and granddaughter in turn. She married Flavius Clemens, cousin of the emperors Titus and Domitian. Their two sons were adopted by Domitian as his successors and given imperial names.

Husband and wife were charged with atheism and Jewish rites, charges that meant they had become Christians. Clemens was put to death, and Domitilla was exiled to Pandataria island. Her burial ground, the Coemeterium Domitillae, was used by Christians as early as the first century. Some sources make her the consul's niece, exiled to Pontia, suggesting two Christian Domitillas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-pan:
Francesco Panigarola, born at Milan on 6 February 1548 and dead at Asti on 31 May 1594, was a Franciscan preacher, controversialist, and Bishop of Asti. As a law student at Pavia and Bologna he lived a dissipated life until grace moved him to enter the Friars Minor at Florence in 1567. At twenty-three his sermons in Rome drew wide attention, and Pius V sent him to Paris for two years to study the Fathers, councils, Greek, and Hebrew. Going back to Italy, he preached for thirteen years in the chief towns.

He converted many Calvinists in France and Savoy, and one sermon at Naples raised enough money to found a hospital for incurables. In 1586 Sixtus V made him titular bishop and coadjutor of Ferrara, transferring him to Asti in 1587. He later served as assistant to the papal legate in France until Henry IV renounced Calvinism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-zab:
Francesco Zabarella, born at Padua on 10 August 1360 and dead at Constance on 26 September 1417, was a cardinal and celebrated canonist of the Great Schism. He studied law at Bologna and Florence, graduating in 1385, and taught canon law at Florence and Padua for twenty-five years. Minor orders only did he ever take, yet he became archpriest of Padua cathedral in 1398. The Paduan government used him on diplomatic missions, including an embassy to Charles VI of France in 1404 against Venice.

When Padua fell to Venice in 1406 he became a loyal Venetian, took part in the Council of Pisa in 1409. He was made Bishop of Florence by John XXIII in 1410 and cardinal deacon in 1411. He was among the most active cardinals of John XXIII and a leading figure at the Council of Constance, where he died before the schism was healed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Avila was a Peruvian priest and investigator of Indian rites, born in Peru as a foundling, his parents unknown, whose date of death is not recorded. He served as curate in Huarochiri province, later at Huanaco, and finally as canon of La Plata, now Sucre, in Bolivia. He was among the most active students of Indian customs of his age. His writings remain a key source for the religion of the Andean peoples under early Spanish rule.

In 1608 he wrote a treatise on the errors, false gods, and superstitions of the Indians of Huarochiri, Mama, and Chaclla. Only the first six chapters survive, translated into English and prized as an invaluable record of Peruvian lore. In 1611 he wrote a report on the Indians of Huanaco, whose manuscript still exists unpublished.

Francisco de Rojas y Zorrilla, born at Toledo on 4 October 1607 and dead in 1680, was a Spanish dramatic poet of the golden age. Authentic facts of his life are fragmentary, but he probably studied at Toledo and Salamanca and served for a time as a soldier. By twenty-five he was already well known as a poet, praised in Montalban's Para todos of 1632. At that moment Lope de Vega, Tirso de Molina, and Calderon stood at the height of their fame.

 He received the mantle of the Order of Santiago in 1644. His plays and autos sacramentales, written alone and with Calderon, Coello, Velez, and Montalban, include Del Rey abajo ninguno, Entre bobos anda el juego, and Casarse por vengarse. They are claimed as the basis of Le Sage's Gil Blas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fussola: Fussola was a titular see in Numidia, a fortified town forty miles from Hippo where Donatists formed most of the people. Saint Augustine named a young man, Antonius, as its first Catholic bishop about 416, and the choice later caused him much worry. A bishop named Melior is known in 484, and the see still stood in the seventh century. Its fortress completed the defenses of Hippo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabala:
Gabala, a titular see of Syria Prima now called Djebeleh, counts ten known bishops between 325 and 553. The most famous are Saint Hilary, writer and martyr of the fourth century, and Severian, first friend and later foe of Saint John Chrysostom. Since the sixth century the city has stood as an exempt archdiocese under the Patriarch of Antioch.

Arabs took Gabala in 639 beside a Byzantine fort, Greeks won it back in 969, and crusaders entered in 1109, setting up a Latin diocese. Saladin seized it in 1187, and Sultan Selim took it in 1517. Today its 3,000 people are all Muslims, but a small harbor, rock chapels, a Roman theater, baths, and a former cathedral mosque still mark its long past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galla:
Galla names the vicariate apostolic of the Oromo tribes in Abyssinia, a vast field between the fourth and tenth parallels north. The Oromo, who began pressing into Abyssinia about the fifteenth century, split into western Borana and eastern Barentouma branches, with many lesser tribes beside. The vicariate dates from May 1846, with the Capuchin Guglielmo Massaia as first vicar.

Massaia reached the Galla country only in November 1852, after five years of hardship and peril. He won converts in Kaffa, gave them priests so the faith would outlast his flights, and later served as confidant to King Menelik at Shoa. Banished seven times, he was made cardinal in 1884 and died in 1889. His successor Taurin built the Harar mission in a stronghold of Islam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-agrico:
George Agricola, a physician, mineralogist, and historian born in Saxony in 1494, earned the title Father of Mineralogy. After wide studies in Germany and Italy, he practiced medicine at Joachimsthal in Bohemia, then moved in 1530 to the Chemnitz mining country at Elector Maurice's call. There he pursued geology and served as Saxon historiographer.

Agricola first approved Luther, but the Reformation's moral fruits and his reading of the Fathers fixed him in the Catholic faith, which he defended boldly among Protestants until his death in 1555. His chief book, On Metals, issued at Basle in 1556, details mining and smelting with curious woodcuts. His Saxon rulers history and an unprinted work on apostolic tradition complete his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-august:
George Augustus Henry Sala, a London journalist born in 1828, lived by his pen from fifteen to his death at Brighton in 1895. Grandson of a Roman who reached England in 1776, he drew, painted scenes, etched, and engraved before journalism claimed him. Dickens took him onto Household Words and All the Year Round, sending him to Russia as special correspondent.

From 1857 Sala wrote for the Daily Telegraph from every corner of the world, much of it reissued in books. His style drew fire as florid, his cookery lore was famous, and his rich earnings melted under costly tastes. His magazine, Sala's Journal, failed and straitened his last years. His love of London, which he knew street by street, marks many books. He entered the Church before death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacinto-plac:
Giacinto Placido Zurla was a Camaldolese monk, scholar, and Cardinal Vicar of Rome, born at Legnano in 1769 and dead at Palermo in 1843. He entered the monastery of San Michele di Murano at eighteen, where he befriended Mauro Cappellari, the future Gregory XVI. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from librarian and writer on medieval geography to high office under three popes.

As librarian he studied Fra Mauro's world map of 1457-1459 and published an account of it in 1806. Further study of early travelers produced his two-volume work on Marco Polo and other Venetian travelers in 1818-19. After Napoleon's suppression of his monastery, he taught theology, became a cardinal in 1821, and served as Cardinal Vicar. He pressed reforms of the Roman seminary, criminal courts, and parishes, winning friends and, through his zeal, some enemies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-baroz:
Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola was an architect of the passage from Renaissance to Baroque, born at Vignola in 1507 and dead in 1573. Pupil and successor of Michelangelo, he wrote two rule books on the classical orders and on practical perspective that guided builders for centuries. A Catholic Encyclopedia article weighs his writings alongside Serlio and Palladio, and his buildings across Italy.

His palace near the Piazza Navona stacked Doric, Ionic, and bracketed cornice stories into a simple, graceful front. The Farnese castle at Viterbo joined a pentagonal fortress outside to a fine circular Renaissance court within. His Gesu in Rome, the first Jesuit church there, joined dome to broad nave and set a plan copied again and again. From 1564 he also carried on Michelangelo's work at St. Peter's, building two lesser domes to his master's plans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran:
Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola was an Italian philosopher, nephew of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, born about 1469 and dead in 1533. Gentle and pious, he was drawn into his family's bitter feuds. He fell with his son Albert at the foot of a crucifix, killed by his nephew Galeotto II after the seizure of Mirandola castle. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a thinker who set philosophy beneath the Bible.

At Rome he defended an eclectic Latin style against the Ciceronian Bembo. Like his uncle he gave himself chiefly to philosophy, but in his Examen of the vanity of Gentile doctrine he lowered the authority of the philosophers, above all Aristotle. He wrote lives of his uncle and of Savonarola, and warned the Lateran Council in 1512 to reform the morals of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-marl:
Giovanni Marliano da Nola was a sculptor and architect born at Nola near Naples in 1488, who died in 1558, though the year is uncertain. Said to be the son of a leather merchant, he studied under Agnolo Aniello Fiore and went to Rome, drawn by Michelangelo's fame. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him a justly praised voice of a rather poor Neapolitan school.

Back in Naples he worked in churches, palaces, and squares. He carved the monument of Galeazzo Pandono in 1514 and tombs of three poisoned youths in 1516. His works include sculptures at Monte Oliveto, the touching recumbent girl Antonia Gandino of 1530, and the Spanish Duke of Cardona's monument at Belpuch. For the viceroy Peter of Toledo he raised a mausoleum in San Giacomo degli Spagnuoli in 1553.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-pico:
Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was an Italian philosopher and scholar born on 24 February 1463, who died on 17 November 1494. Giving his share of the Mirandola principality to his brothers, he went to Bologna at fourteen for canon law, then turned to philosophy and theology. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows seven years of wandering through the universities of Italy and France.

He learned Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic, and, trusting an impostor's sixty Hebrew manuscripts, wove Kabbala fancies into his thought. At Rome in 1486 he offered to defend nine hundred theses on every subject. He offered to pay the travel costs of distant disputants. Innocent VIII had thirteen theses judged heretical, and banned the disputation, and condemned the book despite Pico's Apologia of 1489.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-savo:
Girolamo Savonarola was a Dominican reformer born at Ferrara in 1452, who died at Florence in 1498. Gifted in philosophy and medicine, he heard a sermon on repentance at Faenza in 1474 and at once entered the Dominican Order at Bologna without his parents' knowledge. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a preacher whose zeal for reform made him the ruler of Florence in all but name.

Sent to Florence in 1481 or 1482, he at first made no impression. From 1490 his sermons on the Apocalypse at San Marco drew all Florence. He became prior of San Marco in 1491 and defied Lorenzo de Medici by refusing the customary visit. Condemned after a falsified trial, he was hanged on 23 May 1498 and his body burned, judged not a heretic in matters of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guastalla:
Guastalla, a town and diocese on the Po in Reggio Emilia, was an obscure hamlet until the tenth century, when Gregory V consecrated its church of St. Peter in 998 and Paschal II held a council there in 1106. Control shifted from Reggio to Cremona and Milan, Filippo Maria Visconti made it a county for Guido Torelli in 1406. The Gonzaga held it as a duchy from 1621 to 1746.

Later rulers read like a map of Italian politics. Parma took it in 1748, Pauline Borghese became princess in 1805, and Marie Louise became duchess in 1815. Modena followed in 1848, and the Kingdom of Italy in 1860. In church terms it became an archipresbyterate in 1471, an abbey in 1583, and a bishopric in 1828, with 26 parishes and 65,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hexapla:
The Hexapla was Origen's Old Testament edition, in Hebrew and Greek, called the most colossal critical work of antiquity. Confusion over the true text of Scripture made it urgently needed. The church had adopted the Septuagint, the Greek version. But that text differed from the Hebrew in added books and passages, and in countless small variations from copying, free-handed corrections, translation slips, and a different Hebrew base text.

Origen set the Hebrew text beside the Septuagint and the later Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, so readers could compare them column by column. Aquila aimed above all at literal accuracy, while Symmachus and Theodotion offered fresh renderings near the end of the second century. The entry explains how this vast apparatus tried to restore order to a tangled textual tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imola:
Imola, a diocese suffragan of Bologna, stands by the Santerno river. Sulla the dictator founded it around 82 B.C. under the ancient name Forum Cornelii. Lombards in the seventh century first used the name Imola for the fortress now called Castellaccio, and the town took the fortress's name.

Paul the Deacon records a royal wedding there in 412, joining Atawulf of the Visigoths to Placidia, daughter of Theodosius the Great. Wars passed the town back and forth between Byzantine and barbarian hands during the Gothic war and following the Lombard invasion. Later it came under papal rule with the exarchate. Fausto Alidosi defended it boldly against Saracens and Hungarians in the ninth century, and Troilo Nordiglio grew very powerful in the tenth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-innocenzo-di-:
Imola painter Innocenzo Francucci, born about 1494 and dead at Bologna about 1550, came to Bologna at twelve to study art on a town grant. His home town voted him ten baskets of grain a year in 1506. In 1508 he joined the workshop of Francia, whose register records the boy's entry on the recommendation of two patrons. A stay in Florence under Mariotto Albertinelli likely followed.

Count Giovanni Battista Bentivoglio then invited him to settle at Bologna, where he spent the rest of his life and where most of his works remain. Raphael's influence, the entry says, soon overtook every earlier influence on his style. Readers get a short life of a second-rank Renaissance painter, traced through town records and workshop books rather than legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-rupel:
John of Rupella was a Franciscan theologian of La Rochelle, first of his order to take a theology degree at Paris. Born toward the end of the twelfth century, he entered the Franciscans young and studied at Paris under Alexander of Hales, who presented him for the bachelorship. By 1238 he was a theology master with pupils of his own.

Summoned that year to discuss church benefices, he declared plurality unlawful in general and taught the same in his school. Bernard of Besse called him a professor famed for holiness and learning, solid and useful in writing, and the best preacher of his day. The entry tempers that praise as Franciscan pride. With Alexander he led the movement that deposed Brother Elias in 1239. Under Haymo of Faversham he helped write the Exposition of the Four Masters, approved at Bologna in 1242. He died in 1245, not 1271 as Wadding held.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-francisc:
José Francisco de Isla was a Spanish Jesuit preacher and satirist who lived from 1703 to 1782. He joined the Society of Jesus at sixteen and studied and taught at Salamanca. He won fame as a popular preacher before his superiors set him to writing full time in 1752. When Spain expelled the Jesuits in 1767, he went into exile, first in Corsica and then in the Papal States.

His lasting fame rests on his witty books rather than his sermons. The best known is the novel-like satire about Frey Gerundio, a preacher he called a pulpit Don Quixote. It mocked the decayed state of Spanish preaching and spread across Europe despite condemnation by the Inquisition. This entry traces a lively life and a sharp pen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-anna-m:
Joseph-Anna-Marie de Moyria de Mailla was a French Jesuit missionary and scholar in China who lived from 1669 to 1748. Born at Château Maillac, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1686 and reached China in 1703, mastering Chinese language and writing and studying Chinese histories. Emperor Kangxi set him, with two fellow Jesuits, to survey the provinces of Henan, Zhejiang, and Fujian, plus Formosa.

Pleased with the survey, the emperor made Mailla a mandarin. At fifty he learned Manchu and translated a Manchu version of the great Chinese annals into French, published in Paris from 1777 as the Histoire générale de la Chine in twelve volumes. His work remains a foundation for connected histories of China and gave Europe its first detailed knowledge of the Shuking classic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-padil:
Juan de Padilla was a Franciscan friar and the first martyr of the present United States. He reached Mexico probably in 1528, served as military chaplain under Nuño de Guzmán, and spent 1531 to 1540 preaching among many Indian peoples and founding convents at Tzapotlán and Tuchpán. In 1540 he joined Coronado's march to the Seven Cities.

When Coronado abandoned New Mexico in 1542, Padilla stayed with two friars to evangelize the Tigua on the Rio Grande. Urged on by zeal, he set out northeast with a small party and was killed by natives as he knelt in prayer. The date and place are uncertain, though Vetancurt gives 30 November 1544. Tales of his rising body at Isleta are myth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kabbala:
Kabbala now names a system of esoteric theosophy that played a large part chiefly among Jews after the tenth century. The word first means reception, and then a doctrine received by oral tradition. Only since the eleventh or twelfth century has it named this system, which claims unbroken transmission from patriarchs, prophets, and elders back to the first man. Its two authoritative expositions are the Book of Creation and the Zohar.

The Book of Creation runs to six chapters and thirty-three sections, written as Abraham's monologue. It counts thirty-two paths of wisdom through which God made the universe. The Zohar, the Kabbalists' Bible, comments on the Pentateuch in Aramaic across its fifty-two weekly lessons. Its title means light, from Genesis's opening words, and its doctrine begins with God as En-Soph, the Endless, known only through the Sephiroth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-killala: This 1913 reference article on Killala — the Irish diocese. John Healy gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the northwestern flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Erin's coast. Its ancient see is famed. Its bishops are famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madrid-alcala: A 1913 entry on Madrid-Alcalá — the Spanish diocese. James Grey gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the Manzanares flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Castilian heart. Its 1885 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magin-catala: A 1913 entry on Catalá — the California missionary. Zephyrin Engelhardt recounts his rugged years. His zeal braved the western wilds. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manila: A 1913 entry on Manila — the Philippine archdiocese. Philip Finegan gives its ancient story. Its archbishops guard the bay's flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the far eastern isles. Its 1579 founding is famed. Its archbishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martianus-cap: A 1913 entry on Capella — the African encyclopedist. Paul Lejay honors his famous Nuptials. His pen wedded the seven arts. The schools prized the curious tome. The fifth century knew his name. His 470 death is famed. His Nuptials are famed. His seven liberal arts are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matricula: A 1913 entry on the Matricula — the church register. Maurice Hassett unfolds its ancient lore. It lists the enrolled poor. The churches prized the seemly roll. The clergy keep its form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its enrolled roll is famed. Its 1907 ancient register is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melfi-and-rap: A 1913 entry on Melfi and Rapolla — the Lucanian diocese. Umberto Benigni gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Vulture flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Italian south. Its 11th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micheas-son-o: This 1913 reference article on Micheas ben Jemla — the truthful prophet. Albin Van Hoonacker unfolds his fateful tale. He faced the lying seers. The Book keeps his holy name. The ages bless his memory. Its 1907 study is famed. His truthful word is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monarchia-sic: The Monarchia Sicula was the Norman kings' claim to govern the Sicilian Church like a papal legate, a privilege that shaped the island for centuries. This entry explains its origins, its exercise, and its controversies. Kings as quasi-popes: the privilege let Norman rulers appoint bishops and judge clerics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-boba: Nicolaus Bobadilla was one of the first companions of St. Ignatius, among the founding fathers of the Society of Jesus. This entry traces his missions, his labors, and his place in Jesuit history. A founder of the Jesuits: his missions carried the new order across Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nola: Nola was the see of St. Paulinus, the aristocrat-turned-bishop whose poems made it famous, and tradition credits it with the invention of church bells. This entry covers its bishops, its saint, and its history. The city of bells and poets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nonantola: Nonantola was the great Benedictine abbey of the Modenese, founded by St. Anselm in the 700s. This entry traces its history, its abbots, and its possessions. A Lombard monastery of the first rank: its abbots ruled like princes in the Po valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-sain: The Order of Santiago was Spain's great military order, guarding the pilgrim roads to Compostela. This entry traces its foundation, its knights, and its history. The red sword of the Reconquista: their knights guarded the pilgrim roads of medieval Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orihuela: Orihuela, the Murcian city of the palm groves, became a bishop's see in the 1500s. This entry covers its diocese, its churches, and its history. The faith in the Vega Baja: its cathedral crowns the fertile Segura valley of Murcia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parenzo-pola: Parenzo-Pola, now Poreč and Pula, is the Istrian diocese of the great Euphrasian Basilica. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith on the Adriatic's eastern shore: its golden mosaics proudly rival the very best of old Ravenna's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulinus-of-p: Paulinus of Pella was the Gallo-Roman nobleman whose autobiographical poem Eucharisticos thanks God through a ruined life. This entry covers his career, his poem, and its charm. The poet of gratitude: his moving verses thank God even amid total ruin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-arias-d: Pedrarias Dávila was the ruthless conquistador who founded Panama and ordered Balboa's death. This entry covers his conquests, his cruelty, and his governorship. The scourge of the isthmus: his cold cruelty stained the whole bloody conquest of Panama forevermore in history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pella: Pella was the Decapolis city where Jerusalem's Christians fled before the siege of 70. This entry covers its biblical fame, its bishops, and its ruins. The refuge of the apostolic Church: its faithful Christians fled the doomed city in haste.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-aqui: This biographical entry profiles Peter of Aquila, a Franciscan theologian of the 1300s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Franciscan gallery, preserved among its medieval schoolmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pogla: Pogla was a city of ancient Pisidia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian highlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portiuncula: The Portiuncula is the tiny chapel where St. Francis founded his order. This entry traces its history, the indulgence, and the great pardon. The cradle of the Franciscan family: its great pardon draws the pilgrims yearly in August's fierce heat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolph-agric: Rudolph Agricola was the humanist of the northern Renaissance. This entry notes his learning, his letters, and his influence. The Petrarca of Germany: his learned letters taught the north of Europe in Latin prose in the 1480s' Renaissance of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-galla: St. Galla was the Roman widow of the sixth century. This entry notes her charity, her visions, and her cult. The matron of the Trastevere poor: her gentle hands fed the hungry in Rome's streets in the 500s' decades of the Goths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-gudula: St. Gudula is the patroness of Brussels. This entry notes her legend, her church, and her cult. The virgin of the Senne valley: her ancient shrine crowns Brussels in Belgium's capital in the 1000s' decades of the dukes of Brabant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-petroni: St. Petronilla was the virgin of the Roman catacombs. This entry notes her legend, her basilica, and her cult. The daughter of St. Peter's household: her ancient sarcophagus rests in Rome's basilica of St. Peter in the Vatican's crypt in the 300s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sancho-de-avi: Sancho de Ávila was the bishop of the Spanish sees. This entry notes his Salamanca, his Jaén, and his works. The prelate of the Siglo de Oro: his learned pen served the sees in Spain's Golden Age in the 1500s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-lucia-d: Santa Lucia del Mela became the prelature of Sicily's north coast. This entry covers its prelates, its church, and its history. The faith of the Tyrrhenian towns: its old church crowns the town in Sicily's north in the province of Messina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santiago-de-g: Santiago de Guatemala became the archdiocese of the highland capital. This entry covers its archbishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the volcanic valley: its ruined cathedral crowns Antigua in Guatemala's valley in the highlands of the country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-satala: Satala, the Armenian fortress of the Euphrates, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the eastern frontier: its Roman walls crown the Euphrates in Armenia's west in the highlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simla: Simla became the archdiocese of India's Himalayan hills. This entry covers its archbishops, its churches, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the summer capital: its stone churches serve the hills in India's north in the Himalayas of the Punjab.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew-bob: St. Andrew Bobola was the Jesuit martyr of Poland. This entry traces his missions, his tortures, and his cult. The apostle of the Lithuanian schismatics: his martyr's blood sealed 1657 in the Cossacks of the Ukraine in the revolt of Khmelnytsky.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-attala: St. Attala was the abbot of Bobbio. This entry traces his Columbanus, his abbey, and his fame. The successor of the Irish founder: his great abbey crowned Bobbio in the 610s' Apennines in the Trebbia of the valley in the hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fabiola: St. Fabiola was the penitent widow of Rome. This entry traces her hospital, her Jerome, and her fame. The mother of the Roman charities: her new hospital crowned Ostia in the 390s' port in the city of the Tiber in the mouth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-felix-of-n: St. Felix of Nola was the priest of the Campanian city. This entry traces his prison, his Paulinus, and his cult. The confessor of the Decian persecution: his holy tomb crowned Nola in the 200s of the faith in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-finnian-of: St. Finnian of Movilla was the abbot of the Down school. This entry traces his Columba, his psalter, and his fame. The master of the Irish monks: his great school crowned Movilla in the 540s' Down in the north of the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-of: St. Francis of Paula was the founder of the Minims. This long entry examines his Calabria, his Louis XI, and his fame. The hermit of the Calabrian hills: his new order crowned Paola in the 1450s' Calabria in the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gerard-maj: St. Gerard Majella was the Redemptorist lay brother. This entry traces his Muro, his miracles, and his cult. The wonderworker of the Neapolitan south: his many miracles crowned Muro in the 1750s' Lucania in the south of the kingdom in the hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ignatius-l: St. Ignatius Loyola was the founder of the Jesuits. This very long entry examines his Exercises, his Rome, and his fame. The soldier saint of the Counter-Reformation: his new Company crowned Rome in the 1540s' Gesù in the city of the popes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ludmilla: St. Ludmilla was the martyr duchess of Bohemia. This entry traces her Methodius, her murder, and her cult. The grandmother of the Czech church: her martyr's blood sealed Tetín in the 921 of the veil in the castle of the Berounka.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paula: St. Paula was the widow of Bethlehem. This entry traces her Jerome, her convents, and her fame. The matron of the Latin pilgrims: her twin convents crowned Bethlehem in the 380s' Judea in the grotto of the Nativity in the hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-o: St. Paulinus of Nola was the bishop poet. This long entry examines his letters, his Felix, and his fame. The senator of the Campanian church: his holy see crowned Nola in the 409 of the empire in the city of the Campania.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-teresa-of-: St. Teresa of Avila was the Carmelite doctor. This very long entry examines her Interior Castle, her reform, and her fame. The foundress of the Discalced Carmelites: her great reform crowned Avila in the 1560s' Castile in the Adaja of the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thecla: St. Thecla was the protomartyr virgin. This long entry examines her Paul, her Seleucia, and her cult. The first female martyr of the Church: her holy cave crowned Seleucia in the 100s of the Church in the city of the Calycadnus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-thecla: The Theclae were the virgin martyrs. This entry traces their Seleucia, their caves, and their cults. The protomartyrs of the female sex: their holy caves crowned Seleucia in the 100s of the Church in the city of the Calycadnus in Turkey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-vitalis-a: Vitalis and Agricola were the martyrs of Bologna. This entry traces their Ambrose, their relics, and their cult. The master and the servant: their martyr's blood sealed Bologna in the 300s of the faith in the city of the Reno.

copyright-law-of-the-united-states-of-am:
The United States Copyright Office's Circular 92 prints the copyright law of the United States as contained in Title 17 of the United States Code. The contents open with the constitutional provision that empowers Congress to secure authors' rights for limited times. The chapters then build the whole federal scheme: subject matter and scope, ownership and transfer, duration, notice, deposit and registration, infringement and remedies, importation, and the Copyright Office itself. Later chapters cover licensing, the Copyright Royalty Judges, and protection for vessel hull designs and semiconductor chips.

Unlike a treatise, the circular offers the statute's own words, organized for working use by authors, publishers, and lawyers. Its preface explains the codification and its amendments. Readers get the primary text of American copyright here entire: the law that decides what may be copied, for how long, and what it costs to take what the law reserves.

dracula:
Bram Stoker, an Irish theatre man, wrote this famed novel of the vampire in 1897. He built it from years of notes on lore, maps, and the old tales of the Carpathians. The Count at its heart has since become the most known figure in all horror.

The tale is told in letters, diaries, and news cuts, a form Stoker handles with great skill. Count Dracula comes from his keep in Transylvania to England, and Van Helsing leads the hunt back. The book fixed the rules of the vampire for the modern mind, from fangs to stakes.
emile-zola:
William Dean Howells wrote this appraisal of Emile Zola within weeks of the French novelist's death, arguing that modern speed lets readers judge a writer fairly almost at once. Zola's great epical imagination and ethical force, he says, were already clear while he lived. The essay defends the dead man against easy moral horror.

Howells examines Zola's naturalist creed, the claim to portray fact without choice or limitation, and shows that Zola always chose and limited, as even a map does. That delusion, he argues, caused endless misunderstanding of the novels. The piece captures an American realist measuring a French master, respectfully correcting his theory while honoring his power and honesty.
farewell-nikola: Farewell, Nikola, Guy Boothby's Dr. Nikola finale. The villain's farewell. This book preserves that novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBILiuzzoViola_:
Paul Magnusson reported for the Washington Post that relatives of Viola Liuzzo had filed a two-million-dollar wrongful-death claim against the FBI. Liuzzo was a civil rights worker who was slain in the South. Her family placed legal blame for her death at the Bureau's door.

A claim of that size against a federal agency is an accusation in legal form. It says the family's lawyers believed the FBI bore responsibility, not just the men who fired. Magnusson's article preserves the filing as the public first heard it, one step in the family's long fight over her killing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonPriscill:
A magazine printed Part II of an excerpt from Twenty Letters to a Friend, the forthcoming memoir of Svetlana Alliluyeva. She was Stalin's daughter, and the magazine billed the pages as her intimate recollections. The excerpt is filed in this archive under the name Priscilla Johnson.

Alliluyeva's defection to the West was a sensation, and her memoir promised the dictator's home life from inside the family. Magazines excerpted it in parts to feed that appetite. The pages preserved here are the second installment, Stalin remembered by the daughter who had escaped him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KaiserRobertBla:
Steven V. Roberts wrote about Robert Blair Kaiser and the literary negotiations around Sirhan Sirhan. His piece opens on election night, with Kaiser keeping vigil while Robert Kennedy's fate hung in the balance. From that night it moves to the business that followed: books, rights, and the men bargaining over a killer's story.

An assassination creates a market before it creates a history. Kaiser's negotiations put a price on access to Sirhan, and Roberts examines the dealing in plain view. The piece preserves the publishing scramble that began while the country was still in mourning.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MumfordPamelaLi:
FBI Special Agent Chester C. Orton interviewed Pamela Lillian Mumford on February 24, 1964. Mumford identified Albert Osborne as the man who had sat next to Lee Harvey Oswald on a bus. The bus ran from Nuevo Laredo to Mexico City in the fall of 1963. Osborne also used the name John Howard Bowen.

Oswald's Mexico trip was one of the most investigated journeys in the case. Who sat beside him, and what was said, mattered to agents tracing his contacts. Mumford's identification put a named man in the next seat. The interview preserves her account in the bureau's standard form, one witness statement among thousands gathered that winter.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaysSurveillanc: The Rays surveillance file: a declassified US government document at the Internet Archive, titled but not described.
